fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Professor Andrew Seidl plays a global leadership role as Senior Technical Advisor to the Biodiversity Finance Initiative. Through this work, he supports countries around the world in designing and implementing innovative finance solutions to close critical funding gaps for biodiversity conservation. 
The Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN), led by the United Nations Development Programme, helps governments assess their biodiversity finance needs, reform policies, and mobilize new public and private investment to protect ecosystems and achieve global conservation targets.  Seidl contributes technical expertise in economic valuation, policy design, and finance strategies, helping translate complex environmental challenges into actionable, country-level investment plans. 
His work spans global research, capacity building, and on-the-ground advising, advancing a shift in how nations value nature and integrate biodiversity into economic decision-making. Through BIOFIN, these efforts have contributed to billions of dollars in financing for nature and support a growing international movement to align financial systems with sustainability and conservation goals.

Brief Summary.value: Professor Seidl advises BIOFIN, helping countries design finance solutions for biodiversity, reform policies, and mobilize investment, advancing global efforts to integrate conservation into economic decision-making and policy.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
The Colorado GROW Youth Institute is a statewide program that empowers high school students to explore and address pressing food security challenges locally and globally. Launched in 2024 in partnership with the World Food Prize Foundation, the program engages students in researching a global challenge, producing a paper, and presenting their ideas in roundtable discussions with peers and professionals at the annual event hosted at the CSU Spur campus.
Participants also engage in interactive, hands-on learning and explore academic and career pathways at the intersection of agriculture, sustainability, and food security. Outstanding student presenters are selected to represent Colorado as delegates at the World Food Prize Foundation’s Global Youth Institute. All participants are considered for scholarships to CSU's College of Agricultural Sciences and may apply for additional opportunities provided by the World Food Prize Foundation.
Beyond the annual event, the program fosters continued leadership development for alumni and provides educators with resources and support to integrate the Global Challenge curriculum into their classrooms.

Brief Summary.value: The Colorado GROW Youth Institute empowers high school students to address food security challenges through research, presentations, hands-on learning, and leadership development, with opportunities for scholarships and global engagement.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Steven Fonte works with farming communities in three highland regions (Junín, Huancavelica, and Ayacucho) of the Peruvian Andes to develop sustainable pathways for agroecological intensification.  This work includes the co-development of forage-based fallows, in collaboration with farmers, as well as evaluation of other promising management options (e.g., agroforestry, diversification) to support soil health, long-term productivity and farmer livelihoods.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Fonte collaborates with Peruvian Andean farmers to develop sustainable agroecological practices, including forage-based fallows and agroforestry, aiming to improve soil health, productivity, and farmer livelihoods.

The project is working to refine a soil health tool kit and related products for use in smallholder farming contexts. This work involves continued validation and refinement of tool kit methods, participatory research with farmer groups and collaborating organizations.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Understanding the interplay between biodiversity and climate change is critical for the implementation of effective and lasting solutions to climate change and for maintaining biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people. The USGS was charged by the US Congress in the Fiscal Year 2022 budget with conducting an assessment that characterizes the state of understanding concerning linkages between biodiversity and climate change for the United States. Drivers of biodiversity loss and climate change impacts cross national boundaries, and accordingly the geographic scope of assessment will include neighboring nations, particularly Canada and Mexico. 
Andy Seidl provided direct inputs on transboundary finance mechanisms and policies to the report. USGS is the primary convenor of this assessment with strong involvement from CONAMP and other agencies of the Mexican and Canadian governments and scholars from first nations/Indigenous people.

Brief Summary.value: USGS leads a congressionally mandated assessment on biodiversity-climate change linkages in the US, Canada, and Mexico, with input on transboundary finance and Indigenous perspectives for effective solutions.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Farmers in Malawi face the dual challenges of low income and substantial post-harvest losses. Drying fruit offers a viable solution by preserving produce that would otherwise be wasted and allowing farmers to access high-value markets. However, no existing literature examines the demand for dried fruits in Malawi or the profitability of selling them domestically. This project investigated the economic feasibility of drying watermelon for sale in Malawi.

Brief Summary.value: This project assessed the economic feasibility of drying watermelon in Malawi to reduce post-harvest losses and increase farmer income, addressing gaps in knowledge about domestic dried fruit markets.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
For more than 25 years, Colorado State University and Lincoln University have sustained a dynamic exchange partnership that offers students an immersive, hands-on international learning experience. Participants study in a close-knit academic environment known for its strengths in agriculture, environmental systems, and sustainability, while engaging in field-based coursework and exploring the diverse landscapes of New Zealand.
Each spring semester, a CSU Faculty-in-Residence accompanies students, providing on-site academic support and fostering a strong sense of community abroad. The program also allows students to earn transferable credits while gaining a global perspective and building international networks.
In 2025, the partnership expanded to include a U.S.-based ranch internship funded by Angus New Zealand, offering participants hands-on industry experience and a unique opportunity to connect international study with applied agricultural practice.

Brief Summary.value: CSU and Lincoln University offer an immersive exchange focused on agriculture and sustainability, with fieldwork in New Zealand and a new U.S. ranch internship for hands-on industry experience.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
This research collaboration between Heifer International, Professor Nick Magnan, and other academic collaborators examines how hybrid distance learning can expand access to vocational training for rural women in Nepal. The project focuses on training women to become community animal health workers (CAHWs)—a critical but hard‑to‑access profession in remote areas where women face mobility constraints and heavy household responsibilities. Traditional CAHW certification requires 35 consecutive days away from home, a barrier that limits women’s participation. 
To address this, the team partnered with Heifer International and the Government of Nepal to design a hybrid training model combining short in‑person modules with tablet‑based home learning. Women completed a five‑day orientation and a ten‑day practical livestock module, while the remainder of the curriculum—covering animal health, breeding, disease diagnostics, and bookkeeping—was delivered remotely. 
A randomized evaluation led by Magnan and colleagues found that hybrid training increased completion rates from 30% to 51% without compromising knowledge, skills, or long‑term job performance. Their findings demonstrate that well‑designed distance learning can meaningfully reduce gendered barriers to professional training and expand economic opportunities for rural women in Nepal.

Brief Summary.value: A hybrid distance learning model for rural Nepali women increased completion rates for animal health worker training, reducing gender barriers and expanding economic opportunities without compromising skills or job performance.

Title (Links).value: HYBRID JOB TRAINING IMPROVES PARTICIPATION FOR WOMEN IN NEPAL, STUDY FINDS

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: This short-term CSU faculty-led program in Germany & Austria provides opportunity for students to follow the exploration of European culture and history through immersion in the European equine industry. An international focus on breeding, showing, managing and marketing of the horse is also an important part of this program. Students have opportunities to visit several horse breeding and training facilities, major manufacturers of equipment, as well as observe training sessions, plus a variety of local cultural activities.

Brief Summary.value: This CSU faculty-led program in Germany and Austria immerses students in European equine industry practices, including breeding, management, marketing, facility visits, and cultural activities.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
This CSU faculty-led fall semester program takes students to live and learn in Florence, Italy. Students study Food & Resource Economics through experiential learning opportunities that go beyond the traditional classroom setting.  
Florence is located in the Tuscany region of Italy, on the banks of the Arno River, surrounded by the rolling hills of the Italian countryside. The city has the essence of the Renaissance and stands out for its culture and history. Florence museums, palaces and churches house some of the greatest artistic treasures in the world.  
Coursework integrates economics, policy, and culture, exploring how Italian food and resource-based industries are shaped by history, markets, and sustainability practices. Students engage in experiential learning through field-based activities and required excursions that connect classroom concepts to real-world contexts across Florence and the surrounding countryside. 
Beyond academics, participants experience daily life in Italy—gaining firsthand insight into local food systems, regional culture, and the role of place in economic development—while building a global perspective on agriculture, sustainability, and international markets.

Brief Summary.value: CSU’s fall program in Florence immerses students in Food & Resource Economics through experiential learning, integrating coursework, field activities, and cultural experiences to explore Italian agriculture, sustainability, and markets.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: This CSU faculty-led summer program gives participants direct exposure to the rich history of landscape design in Italy and France. Students will visit many important landscape architectural precedents and pursue research on various topics including land planning, urban design, community design, and insightful garden design for public and private places. Students will travel throughout Italy and France to explore architecture in many different cities including Venice, Tuscany, Florence, Rome, Versailles, Normandy and Paris. Specific site visits may include classical landscapes in and around Rome, medieval hill towns of Tuscany, remarkable private gardens and villas of the renaissance near Florence, royal parks of Louis XIV in central France, and the modern public gardens of Paris.

Brief Summary.value: CSU faculty-led summer program offers students hands-on study of historic landscape design in Italy and France, including site visits, research, and exploration of urban and garden design.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
The University of Glasgow's School of Veterinary Medicine, has an internationally renowned reputation in Veterinary Medicine, and is fully accredited by the AVMA. CSU is working with The University of Glasgow to offer a unique opportunity for high quality animal science and equine science students who wish to study veterinary medicine within the global context.
Selected students will study the final year of their animal science/equine science degree at the University of Glasgow as a study abroad opportunity. During their time at Glasgow, CSU students will study alongside students in their first year of the University of Glasgow’s veterinary medicine degree programme (Bachelor of Veterinary Medicine and Surgery, BVMS – which is the equivalent to the DVM).

Brief Summary.value: CSU partners with University of Glasgow to offer animal and equine science students a study abroad year, integrating with Glasgow’s veterinary medicine program for global veterinary education experience.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
A sabbatical at Chalmers University in Gothenburg, Sweden--in the Chalmers School of Entrepreneurship--inspired both a new graduate program and a new line of research at CSU. 
The masters in Agribusiness and Food Innovation Management was developed by Dr. Graff and colleagues in the department of Agricultural and Resource Economics to be offered at CSU Spur. The program adapted key design elements from the Chalmers masters in entrepreneurship, including a team-based degree project in which students develop and seek to launch a new product, technology, or even a startup. Instructors in Sweden have regularly provided guest lectures in this CSU program.
Dr. Graff has also collaborated with faculty and Ph.D. students at Chalmers on research to understand how the dynamics of the venture financing lifecycle influences the success and thus the economic impact of startups. This line of research led to a recently published study on the venture financing of agtech startups in the U.S.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Graff’s sabbatical at Chalmers inspired CSU’s new Agribusiness master’s program and research on venture financing, fostering international collaboration and innovative, team-based student projects.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Faculty from the Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics regularly participate in a faculty exchange with had Vietnam's Foreign Trade University. 
Established in 2008, the CSU-FTU Vietnam Economics Curriculum Project originated as a curriculum development initiative, specifically to help FTU align its undergraduate curriculum with international norms. The project was established and supported by Vietnam’s Ministry of Education and Training, who funded parts of the project for the first three years.
As it evolved under the leadership of CSU Professor of Economics Bob Kling, the program became a multi-dimensional partnership between the universities. Since 2014, more than 1,000 FTU students have taken courses from CSU faculty in Hanoi, while almost 200 FTU students have transferred to CSU to complete their CSU degree.
Beyond the success of the core programming, CSU has welcomed more than a dozen FTU graduates and FTU faculty members into its graduate Economics programs; provided short-term research methods training for visiting scholars; and extended cooperation to also include Vietnam Forestry University and Vietnam Water Resources University.

Brief Summary.value: Since 2008, CSU and FTU have partnered to align FTU’s economics curriculum with international standards, resulting in student exchanges, faculty collaboration, and expanded cooperation with other Vietnamese universities.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
For the approximately three quarters of the world’s poor who live in rural areas of low-income countries, agriculture and livestock are key for household income and economic growth. Opportunities to sell livestock to meat producers for revenue offer a channel for households to turn illiquid assets into liquid ones, bolstering household income and enabling consumption smoothing. Livestock are therefore an important asset and caring for their health is an economic investment. And yet, households face constraints in caring for their livestock and selling them. Veterinary care for household animals in poor, rural areas is limited, constrained by a low supply of knowledgeable animal health workers. Rural households face challenges in coordinating and executing sales to meat producers, constrained by diffuse communication networks and information asymmetries between buyers and sellers.
In this study, Dr. Magnan used a randomized controlled trial to test the effect of the introduction of two novel digital technologies to livestock cooperatives in rural Nepal. The first tool, an app ecosystem called “Digital Collective Marketing” is aimed at reducing information frictions in the market for goats raised by farmers in rural cooperatives and sold to urban meat producers. The second tool, a mobile app called “Digital Mentoring and Continuing Education”, is aimed at improving the knowledge and skills of community animal health workers who care for the health of the goats of farmers in these cooperatives.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Magnan’s study tested two digital tools in rural Nepal to improve goat sales and animal health by reducing market information gaps and enhancing animal health worker training in cooperatives.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: The Weed Science Lab's partnership with Brazilian universities represents a research network built over more than 20 years, anchored by strong ties to Universidade Federal Rural do Rio de Janeiro, the Federal University of Pelotas, and Universidade de São Paulo's Piracicaba campus. Over time, the partnership has produced a steady flow of student exchange — undergraduate interns, "sandwich" PhD students who conduct research at CSU while earning their degrees from their home institutions, and students who complete a master's degree and/or a PhD from CSU. That continuity has made the lab a known destination: students from Brazil understand the lab is a place where they can plug in, contribute, and grow.  At the heart of the shared research is herbicide resistance, studied through genomic approaches.

Brief Summary.value: The Weed Science Lab’s 20-year partnership with Brazilian universities fosters student exchanges and collaborative research on herbicide resistance using genomics, making the lab a recognized destination for Brazilian students.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Professor Todd Gaines serves as director of the International Weed Genomics Consortium (IWGC), a global collaboration that brings together researchers, industry partners, and agricultural professionals to advance the understanding of weed biology through genomics. Founded in 2021 with support from the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR) and industry sponsors, the consortium addresses weed management as a worldwide agricultural challenge by developing genomic resources that are openly available to researchers across the globe. Under Gaines’ leadership, the IWGC provides scientific guidance for genome sequencing and annotation projects, facilitates international collaborations, and connects researchers to opportunities for training, publications, and shared research initiatives. The consortium has grown into a network of more than 500 scientists and stakeholders spanning over 50 countries. 
In addition to leading the consortium’s scientific agenda, Gaines plays a key role in building the global weed science community through conferences, workshops, and training programs. The IWGC regularly hosts educational events that help researchers and students develop expertise in genomics tools and applications, while also creating opportunities to establish new international partnerships. Since its launch, the consortium has become a recognized leader in weed genomics, supporting the sequencing of dozens of economically important weed species and providing a platform where scientists can share data, resources, and best practices. Through this combination of leadership, training, and community-building, Gaines has helped position the IWGC as a central hub for advancing weed science worldwide.

Brief Summary.value: Professor Todd Gaines leads the International Weed Genomics Consortium, advancing global weed genomics research, training, and collaboration, supporting genome sequencing, and building a worldwide network of scientists and stakeholders.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Todd Gaines has developed a robust international research network that integrates industry, government, and academic partners to address herbicide resistance and weed genomics.  In Germany, his collaborations with Bayer Crop Science, BASF, and the Julius Kühn Institute have supported joint research projects, student training, and exchange visits. His contributions to understanding the biology and genomics of Apera spica-venti—a major grass weed affecting cereals in Eastern Europe—have helped advance genome research and practical management strategies.  In the United Kingdom, Gaines partners with Rothamsted Research on grant-funded initiatives that enable joint lab meetings, faculty and student exchanges, and shared training resources, including recorded educational materials. These efforts are strengthened by leadership roles in global genomics consortia, further expanding collaborative impact. Gaines’ work in Australia reflects long-standing partnerships with leading herbicide resistance programs, including the Australian Herbicide Resistance Initiative at the University of Western Australia and collaborations with Adelaide University. These engagements emphasize faculty exchange, joint research, and international workshops on weed genomics, while also creating career pathways for graduate students. Emerging collaborations in Asia, including a workshop offered at Seoul National University, highlight growing connections in herbicide resistance and precision agriculture research. Additional partnerships in Japan continue to broaden research opportunities.  Across these regions, Gaines’ global engagement fosters knowledge exchange, builds research capacity, and trains the next generation of scientists tackling critical challenges in agricultural sustainability.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Gaines leads international collaborations with industry, government, and academia to advance herbicide resistance and weed genomics, supporting research, training, and knowledge exchange across Europe, Australia, and Asia.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Professor Andales joined engineers and scientists from Colorado State University, the Israel Institute of Technology, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and government officials from the U.S. and Israel to participate in the Sustainable Agricultural Water Workshop. 
The workshop focused on how Israel and the western U.S. have similar semi-arid climates and a common interest in water sustainability, which allowed both nations to think reflectively about the challenges and opportunities for sustainable agricultural water.

Brief Summary.value: Professor Andales joined U.S. and Israeli experts at a workshop to discuss shared challenges and opportunities for sustainable agricultural water in semi-arid climates.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Jennifer Bousselot, an expert on urban agriculture, studies how plants respond to rooftop growing conditions to determine how unused urban spaces can be used to produce food and even generate energy simultaneously through rooftop agrivoltaics. Her research has taken her around the world to study how other countries utilize rooftop gardening and to share her expertise with international audiences, including presentations in Europe and the Middle East. In spring 2024, Jennifer taught courses aboard Semester at Sea, traveling to nine ports across Asia, Africa, and Europe while leading field experiences for her three classes. She is also currently finalizing a chapter for a sustainability book led by collaborators in Asia and Australia, and she routinely peer reviews related research from every continent.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Jennifer Bousselot researches rooftop agrivoltaics, teaches globally, and collaborates internationally to advance urban agriculture, sustainability, and food production using underutilized urban spaces.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: The North American Agricultural Advisory Network (NAAAN) is a regional platform that brings together extension and advisory service professionals from the United States, Canada, and Mexico to strengthen agricultural knowledge systems. As part of the broader Global Forum for Rural Advisory Services (GFRAS), NAAAN represents one of 18 networks. NAAAN promotes collaboration, information-sharing, and capacity development among institutions and practitioners working in agricultural extension, education, and outreach. The network supports cross-border dialogue on best practices, innovation, policy, and areas requiring technical expertise with the goal of enhancing the effectiveness of advisory services and advancing sustainable, resilient agricultural systems and food security across North America. The Secretariat for the NAAAN is hosted by the Colorado State University System in partnership with the College of Agricultural Sciences.

Brief Summary.value: NAAAN unites US, Canada, and Mexico extension professionals to share knowledge, foster collaboration, and advance sustainable agriculture through cross-border dialogue, innovation, and capacity building. Hosted by CSU.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
The key differences between introduced species that become harmful invaders and those who do not is an ongoing research question. In this project, Hufbauer and colleagues from France, New Zealand, and Australia study whether species that adapt to human-altered environments in their native regions are more likely to thrive in similar environments when introduced elsewhere.
By combining field sampling, genetic analysis, and environmental data, the team examines how human activities—such as land use change—shape the traits that help species spread. Their findings show how these human-driven conditions can create predictable patterns that favor certain species becoming invasive.
This research helps scientists better understand and anticipate biological invasions, improving our ability to prevent and manage invasive species that can harm ecosystems, agriculture, and economies.

Brief Summary.value: Researchers study if species adapted to human-altered environments in their native regions are more likely to become invasive elsewhere, using fieldwork and genetics to predict and manage biological invasions.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Under a sub-contract from the University of Utah, CSU contributed to research mentorship and curriculum development for the Hydraulics, Irrigation, and Drainage MS degree program at the U.S.- Pakistan Center for Advanced Studies in Water. The U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) provided 5-years of funding to Mehran University of Engineering and Technology and University of Utah, USA to establish the center. Dr. Andales collaborated with Dr. Timothy Gates and Dr. Jose L. Chavez in Civil and Environmental Engineering to provide research and curricular training to the faculty, staff, and students at Mehran University of Engineering and Tehcnology. From 2016 to 2019, Dr. Andales hosted a total of six visiting scholars from the Center for Advanced Studies in Water for one-semester periods at CSU, where they were mentored in irrigation management and field or lab research methods.

Brief Summary.value: CSU supported curriculum development and research mentorship for a Pakistan-based MS program in water studies, hosting six visiting scholars for training in irrigation management and research methods from 2016-2019.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: The Borowiec lab studies ants from around the world in collaboration with researchers from multiple countries to understand how ants evolved and became so diverse and successful. The lab uses large-scale DNA data to build detailed evolutionary trees, showing both how different groups are related and how similar traits evolve independently in different groups. This work helps explain broad patterns in biodiversity and how species adapt to their environments, which is important for understanding ecosystems globally.

Brief Summary.value: The Borowiec lab uses global DNA data to map ant evolution, revealing relationships, trait development, and biodiversity patterns, aiding understanding of species adaptation and ecosystem function worldwide.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: The CSU Potato Improvement Program shares potato germplasm and exchanges unselected seedling potato families with the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada National Potato Breeding Program at the Fredericton Research and Development Centre. This collaboration allows the program to broaden the genetic diversity of the parental material, ensuring the development of resilient potato varieties. The exchange of unselected material between the Canada Potato Breeding Program and CSU is an efficient method to produce a high volume of seedling tubers, as well as increasing the likelihood of identifying elite cultivars adapted to either region, benefiting both programs.

Brief Summary.value: CSU collaborates with Canada’s Potato Breeding Program to exchange germplasm, broadening genetic diversity and efficiently developing resilient, regionally adapted potato varieties for mutual benefit.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Professor Jessica Prenni’s international research collaborations are centered on the Periodic Table of Food Initiative (PTFI), which aims to standardize the characterization of food composition across the world’s edible biodiversity. Her work involves analytical studies of foods and close collaboration with international partners, including training in laboratory methods, joint data analysis, and co-authorship of scientific publications. Through these efforts, she contributes to building a global research ecosystem focused on improving understanding of food quality to address interconnected challenges in human and planetary health. Her collaborations also emphasize education, mentorship, and capacity building for early-career scientists, particularly in the Global South.

Brief Summary.value: Professor Prenni collaborates internationally on the Periodic Table of Food Initiative, standardizing food composition analysis, advancing global research, and supporting education and capacity building for early-career scientists.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Keith Belk is a founding contributor to an international effort focused on ensuring that livestock and meat policies are informed by scientific evidence. At a conference in 2022, the group created the Dublin Declaration, a document defending the role of livestock in society and calling for policies affecting livestock to be based on reliable evidence to achieve balance in the future of livestock. Dr. Belk later hosted a second meeting in 2024 that resulted in the Denver Call for Action encouraging policy-makers to focus on science based nutrition guidelines, avoid over-generalizations when discussing livestock systems, and respect the science behind livestock systems. Since those meetings, there have been international discussions and conventions of scientists, policymakers, and industry leaders from around the world to address the environmental, nutritional, ethical, and societal roles of livestock production.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Belk led international efforts advocating for science-based livestock policies, resulting in the Dublin Declaration and Denver Call for Action, promoting evidence-based guidelines and balanced discussions on livestock’s societal roles.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
The Ant Course is a globally recognized training program that brings together students, researchers, and professionals to learn directly from leading myrmecologists through a combination of lectures, laboratory work, and hands-on field experience. Participants gain practical skills in ant identification, sampling, specimen curation, and the study of ant diversity, behavior, and their roles in ecosystems. The October 2026 Ant Course will take place at CSU's Todos Santos campus in Mexico.
The course emphasizes ant phylogeny, diversity, and classification; social behavior and colony biology; field collection and biodiversity sampling methods; and specimen preparation and identification techniques.
The program is designed for a broad audience, including students, postdocs, professors, researchers, and motivated participants from diverse backgrounds in biology, including those with no previous experience with ants.

Brief Summary.value: The Ant Course at CSU Todos Santos offers hands-on training in ant identification, diversity, behavior, and field methods for students, researchers, and professionals from diverse biology backgrounds.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Dr. Amanda Countryman's research investigates how international trade and trade policy influence agricultural markets, rural economies, and environmental outcomes. Through economic modeling and collaborative research with domestic and international partners, she analyzes the implications of trade agreements, tariffs, market access, supply chain disruptions, and other policy interventions affecting agriculture.
Recent studies have examined the effects of international trade policy on rural employment and wages, trade competitiveness in agricultural sectors, global commodity markets, food system resilience, and the environmental implications of agricultural production and trade. Her work contributes to a broader understanding of how international economic policies shape agricultural opportunities and challenges around the world.
Collaborating with researchers, policymakers, and stakeholders across multiple countries, Dr. Countryman's work helps connect Colorado and U.S. agriculture to global markets and policy discussions. The results of this research help inform trade policy discussions and support more effective decision-making by governments, industry organizations, and agricultural stakeholders.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Countryman’s research analyzes how international trade policies impact agricultural markets, rural economies, and the environment, informing policy decisions and connecting U.S. agriculture to global markets and discussions.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
AI is a relatively new technology that is being tested as a platform for herbicide discovery. One of the leading company using this technology to discovery new modes of action is Agrematch, an Israel-based company using AI to solve chemistry problems across disciplines. Dr. Franck Dayan has been collaborating with this company to validate the modes of action that have been flagged by their algorithm. 
This project with Agrematch validated the mode of action of novel herbicides as PPO inhibitors, meaning that they block an enzyme from being formed, eventually leading to a buildup of toxic compounds and the death of the weed. While the mode of action of these structures is not novel, the algorithm identified structures that would not be expected to target this enzyme. 
They also discovered a natural herbicide that inhibits photosynthesis in a manner similar to paraquat, an herbicide that interrupts the electron transport chain, leading to destruction of the cell membranes. Paraquat is one of the most toxic herbicides, with just 1 teaspoon being lethal to adults and no known antidote.  Due to its dangerous effect on humans, registration is being revoked around the world. In contrast, this natural product, rhein, is very safe and found in a number of food sources. 
From these research efforts, two grad students were able to author publications and use their experiences to pursue further opportunities in their field.

Brief Summary.value: AI-driven collaboration with Agrematch validated novel herbicide modes of action, identified safer natural alternatives to toxic herbicides, and provided graduate students with research and publication opportunities.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Through a USDA NIFA-funded partnership with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines, University Distinguished Professor Jan Leach's lab is exploring an overlooked question: how do disease-resistant rice plants affect not just harmful pathogens, but also the beneficial microbes that live in, on and around the plant. The issue is similar to what happens in humans when we take antibiotics. While antibiotics kill harmful bacteria, they can also disrupt the body’s healthy microbial community. 
The Leach lab is asking whether breeding crops for disease resistance has a similar unintended effect. When plants are bred to resist disease, they activate defense responses that produce chemicals that help fight off pathogens—but those same chemicals may also reshape the plant’s microbiome. Until now, little attention has been paid to these broader impacts. To address this gap, the team is studying rice plants with different resistance genes and tracking how their microbial communities change over time. They are also examining how these changes affect plant health and performance in the long term. 
This work has implications beyond plant disease. Rice paddies are one of the world's largest agricultural sources of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Methane is produced not by the rice plants themselves, but by specialized microbes living in the flooded soil and around rice roots. The composition of these microbial communities can influence how much methane is generated and released into the atmosphere. By understanding how disease-resistance traits alter plant-associated microbial communities, researchers may uncover new strategies to reduce methane emissions while maintaining strong disease resistance. 
In collaboration with partners in Taiwan, the CSU-IRRI team is measuring how resistance-related changes in the rice microbiome affect methane production and emissions. Together, this research is opening a new way of thinking about crop improvement—one that considers not only the genetics of the plant, but also the microbial communities that support it, with important implications for both global food security and climate resilience.

Brief Summary.value: Leach lab studies how breeding rice for disease resistance impacts beneficial microbes and methane emissions, aiming to improve crop health and reduce greenhouse gases for food security and climate resilience.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: University Distinguished Professor Jan Leach serves as a Board Member for the International Phytobiomes Alliance, an international, nonprofit alliance of industry, academic, and governmental partners that facilitates and coordinates international efforts toward expanding phytobiomes research. A phytobiome refers to the complex ecosystem formed by plants and their surrounding environment, including microbes, insects, animals, and other plants. By promoting phytobiome health, the Alliance supports more resilient and sustainable agricultural systems. Its work emphasizes how management decisions—from irrigation and pest control to crop breeding—shape these systems, and it provides research and education to help producers apply phytobiome-based practices in diverse global contexts.

Brief Summary.value: University Distinguished Professor Jan Leach serves on the International Phytobiomes Alliance Board, supporting global research and education to promote resilient, sustainable agriculture through phytobiome-based management and practices.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Plant breeders have traditionally focused on single disease resistance genes—acting as “generals”—that detect pathogens and signal downstream genes to mount a defense response. However, pathogens evolve over time to overcome these resistance genes, limiting the durability of this strategy. To address this challenge, University Distinguished Professor Jan Leach's lab is advancing a novel approach that shifts focus from the “generals” to the downstream “soldier” genes that execute defense responses. 
Rather than relying on pathogen recognition alone, this strategy enhances how effectively defense genes respond once triggered. By selecting for stronger gene promoters, the team aims to amplify and broaden activation of defense pathways, resulting in more robust and durable resistance. As Leach notes, “It actually works—we’ve shown we can select for better promoters of those genes, and it makes the plants more resistant.” 
Support from the Foundation for Food and Agricultural Research has enabled an ongoing international collaboration with the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) in Colombia. This partnership includes Colorado State University, the Universidad de Los Andes (Colombia), and the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD). The project has delivered both scientific and capacity-building outcomes. It has generated genome sequences of key rice varieties and demonstrated the ability to identify and target genomic regions associated with enhanced defense responses. It has also trained graduate students and research associates across partner institutions and CGIAR centers. A three-day workshop at CIAT introduced plant breeders from across Latin America to this new strategy. Importantly, the project has fostered new and ongoing interdisciplinary and international collaborations.

Brief Summary.value: Leach’s lab developed a novel approach to plant disease resistance by enhancing defense gene promoters, resulting in more durable resistance and international collaborations, training, and scientific advances in rice breeding.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: A growing share of the world’s rice is produced in Africa, where a destructive pathogen studied by the University Distinguished Professor Jan Leach's lab is causing significant and expanding damage. To address this emerging threat, the lab is working closely with the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD). In Tanzania and neighboring countries, IRD researchers have used diagnostic tools (primers) developed by the Leach lab to confirm the presence of the pathogen, which continues to spread across the region. This collaboration has been critical in tracking the disease and understanding its impact on rice production. Dr. Leach contributes to global efforts to combat the pathogen by serving on a scientific advisory committee for a Gates Foundation–supported project focused on developing new forms of resistance. These efforts are now reaching a key milestone: newly developed resistant rice varieties are expected to be released soon, offering farmers a much-needed tool to protect their crops and livelihoods.

Brief Summary.value: Leach lab collaborates internationally to track and combat a destructive rice pathogen in Africa, leading to the imminent release of resistant rice varieties to protect regional agriculture.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: The Herbicide Selectivity and Action course (AB 509) has become a go-to resource for learners worldwide seeking to build or refresh expertise in herbicide science. Delivered fully online and asynchronously over a 16-week semester, the course consistently draws an international mix of graduate students and industry professionals, including company leaders who have transitioned into roles requiring a deeper understanding of herbicides. Designed to be flexible yet rigorous, the course emphasizes peer-to-peer learning, with participants actively engaging across sectors and geographies as they progress through the material. With steady enrollment and growing visibility through professional networks and industry outreach, the course serves as a unique platform for continuing education in weed science. Its structure enables participants to immediately apply concepts in real-world settings, while also fostering a collaborative learning environment that connects academia and industry. Through this model, Dayan and Gaines have expanded access to specialized training and strengthened global knowledge exchange in herbicide resistance.

Brief Summary.value: AB 509 is a fully online, 16-week course attracting global graduate students and professionals, fostering peer learning and immediate application of herbicide science concepts in academic and industry settings.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Franck Dayan is a leading researcher advancing the understanding of herbicides and herbicide resistance. His work focuses on discovering how herbicides function at the biochemical and molecular levels, identifying new herbicide targets, and developing strategies to combat the growing problem of herbicide-resistant weeds. In a project sponsored by Bayer, Dayan and a graduate student, Hudson Takano, investigated the molecular effects of an herbicide called glufosinate, which causes plants to build up a toxic chemical, eventually kiling it.  By combining glufosinate with another type of herbicide, PPO herbicide, they discovered a way to kill weeds with significantly less herbicides, only 1/2 of the glufosinate and 1/30 of the PPO herbicide for the same level of effectiveness. This research resulted in patents held internationally for the combination of the herbicides. Dayan's research supports the development of more effective and sustainable weed management practices, helping protect agricultural productivity while reducing the long-term impacts of herbicide resistance.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Dayan’s research discovered that combining glufosinate and PPO herbicides effectively controls weeds with lower doses, supporting sustainable weed management and resulting in internationally held patents.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Quinoa is a traditional Andean crop with increasing global importance because of its nutritional value, drought tolerance, and potential role in climate-resilient agriculture. As quinoa production expands beyond its center of origin, however, growers are encountering new pest challenges that require locally adapted integrated pest management strategies. This project connects emerging quinoa pest issues in North America with the longer history of quinoa cultivation and pest management in Peru and the broader Andean region.
In collaboration with Prof. Luis Miguel Cruces at the Universidad Nacional Agraria La Molina in Lima, Peru, Dr. Szczepaniec's team is comparing quinoa pest management across Andean and North American production systems. This work has led to a collaborative manuscript, _Quinoa pest management across continents: Lessons from Andean systems and emerging threats in North America_, which examines how pest complexes differ between long-established Andean systems and newer quinoa production regions in the United States. The project highlights shared priorities, including improved monitoring, biological control, host plant resistance, and regionally appropriate IPM tools. 
This collaboration is also creating a foundation for future comparative research on whether quinoa varieties grown in Peru may express stronger resistance to emerging pests affecting quinoa production in the United States, including the stem-boring fly _Amauromyza karli_. More broadly, the project supports international scholarly exchange and helps build pest management strategies informed by both Andean experience and emerging North American production needs.

Brief Summary.value: This project compares quinoa pest management in Andean and North American systems, identifying shared priorities and fostering international collaboration to develop regionally adapted, climate-resilient integrated pest management strategies.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Pablo Pinedo collaborates with DeLaval, a Swedish leader in robotic milking technology, to advance research on dairy cow health, behavior, and well-being in automated milking systems. These technologies generate extensive data on individual cows during each milking event, providing valuable insights that support both on-farm management and scientific discovery. Research conducted through this partnership has explored topics such as cow preferences when selecting milking units and the health outcomes associated with different milking behaviors. In addition to supporting research, DeLaval has provided support for two graduate students who have worked on the studies. By transforming farm-generated data into actionable knowledge, the collaboration helps develop evidence-based management strategies that improve animal welfare, productivity, and decision-making for dairy producers.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Pablo Pinedo partners with DeLaval to research dairy cow health and behavior in robotic milking systems, generating data that informs evidence-based management and supports graduate student research.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
CSU and Lincoln University (NZ) signed an International Memorandum of Understanding in 2026 to build on the 25 year old undergraduate student exchange program. The Global Rams Family scholarly mobility program will expand this relationship to include research cooperation between the two institutions.  The initial focus is on agrivoltaics systems and their contribution to sustainable food and energy production.  Agrivoltaics is the combination of the words "agriculture" and "photovoltaics" (aka solar energy), and the practice of combining the two on the same plot of land.
The Global Rams Family program will facilitate student and scholar mobility, enabling the exchange of knowledge, research experiences, and agrivoltaics best practices between the two institutions.  Selected scholars will travel to New Zealand for approximately 2-4 weeks in January each year.  CSU Scholars will also help to host New Zealand visiting scholars who travel to Colorado in June each year.  Scholars will be predominantly graduate students in the first few years of the program.

Brief Summary.value: CSU and Lincoln University expanded their partnership to include research and scholar exchanges focused on agrivoltaics, promoting sustainable food and energy production through annual graduate student and scholar mobility programs.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
The North American Agricultural Advisory Network (NAAAN) is hosting a first of its kind tri-national meeting in Regina, Saskatchewan May 11-13, 2027. 
Extension and rural advisory services play an important and unique role in the agricultural systems of Canada, Mexico, and the United States. The 2022 NAAAN baseline report, Feeding North America through Agricultural Extension, established a shared understanding of how extension contributes to the agricultural development of the three countries. 

Building on that foundation, the 2027 Regina Convening will explore the future of extension and rural advisory services across North America – Addressing Challenges to Thrive. The convening is grounded in the recognition that many of the region’s most pressing challenges are shared. Pathogens, natural disasters, and extreme weather events don’t stop at national borders. By sharing knowledge, innovations, and response strategies across the continent, we can help strengthen resilience and food security. 

The convening is designed to foster strategic awareness and collaboration in extension and rural advisory services among business leaders, policymakers, researchers, producers, and community organizations across: 
·        Emerging technologies
·        Creative financing for agriculture 
·        Biodefense and disaster preparedness
·        Water management and soil health

Brief Summary.value: NAAAN’s 2027 tri-national meeting in Regina will unite leaders to address shared agricultural challenges, focusing on extension services, technology, financing, biodefense, disaster preparedness, and resource management.
